subject: Cloud Computing
title: CDNs and Edge Caching
description: A micro-lesson that makes CDNs and Edge Caching usable.

hook.text: Your website loads in 100ms from New York but 3 seconds from Sydney. A CDN fixes that distance problem.

buildup.text: A Content Delivery Network caches content at hundreds of locations worldwide, close to where users actually are.

discovery.text: CloudFront, Cloudflare, and Akamai serve images, scripts, and pages from the nearest edge location.

twist.text: CDNs work great for static content. Dynamic, personalized content is harder — you can't cache what differs per user.

climax.text: Modern CDNs now run code at the edge. Cloudflare Workers and Lambda@Edge process requests without a central server.

punchline.text: Bring the content closer to the user. Speed is distance.

quiz.question: What limits CDN effectiveness for dynamic content?
options: Personalized content differs per user and cannot be cached generically
CDNs can only store images, not HTML or JavaScript
Dynamic content is too small to benefit from caching

details.summary: Content delivery networks cache static and dynamic content at edge locations worldwide, serving users from the nearest point of presence. This reduces latency, offloads origin servers, and improves availability by distributing content globally.
details.whyItMatters: A CDN can cut page load times by 50 percent or more for global audiences. It is the simplest way to improve performance without changing application code.
takeaways: Content is served from the edge location nearest the user
Origin server load is dramatically reduced
Global availability improves even if the origin goes down

faq.question: Can CDNs cache dynamic content?
faq.answer: Yes. Modern CDNs can cache API responses, personalized pages with edge compute, and dynamic content with short TTLs. Edge functions from providers like Cloudflare Workers and AWS CloudFront Functions enable custom logic at the edge.

faq.question: How does CDN cache invalidation work?
faq.answer: You can purge specific URLs, use wildcard purges, or set cache-control headers with short TTLs. Most CDNs complete purges within seconds. Versioned URLs with content hashes in the filename avoid invalidation entirely by using unique URLs for each version.
